'''Barbara Hope Cooper''' (September 1, 1953 – August 7, 1999)<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Ashcroft|first1=Neil|last2=Fitchen|first2=Douglas|last3=Ho|first3=Wilson|date=2000-04-01|title=Barbara Hope Cooper|journal=Physics Today|volume=53|issue=4|pages=84–86|doi=10.1063/1.883057|issn=0031-9228|doi-access=free}}</ref> was an American physicist. She was the first female professor on the physics faculty at [[Cornell University]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Barbara Hope Cooper, first woman physics professor at Cornell University, dies at 45|url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/1999/08/barbara-hope-cooper-first-woman-physics-professor-cornell-dies-45|access-date=2021-05-06|website=Cornell Chronicle|language=en}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Feibelman|first=Peter J.|date=2000|title=Barbara Cooper|url=https://aps.org/programs/women/reports/gazette/upload/spring00.pdf|journal=CSWP Gazette|volume=19|pages=4}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Cooper was born in [[Lancaster, Pennsylvania|Lancaster]] in 1953. She was raised in [[Newark, Delaware|Newark]]. She attended [[Newark High School (Delaware)|Newark High School]] and graduated in 1971.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=BARBARA COOPER Obituary (2008) - Wilmington, DE - The News Journal|url=https://www.legacy.com/amp/obituaries/delawareonline/145543682|access-date=2021-05-06|website=www.legacy.com|language=en}}</ref> Her father, Charles Burleigh Cooper, was an emeritus professor of physics at the [[University of Delaware]]. She completed her undergraduate degree in 1976 at [[Cornell University]]. When she started at Cornell, she intended to apply to medical school. When she injured her back in her second year, she took a break from her studies to recover and was hired to work on an undergraduate research project at the Cornell Laboratory of Nuclear Studies. She became more interested in physics.<ref name=":0" /> She went on to obtain a PhD from the [[California Institute of Technology]] in 1982.<ref name=":2" /> She was supervised by Thomas Tombrello. Her thesis was entitled ''Erosion of Ice Films by Energetic Ions''.<ref>{{Cite thesis|title=Erosion of Ice Films by Energetic Ions|url=https://resolver.caltech.edu/CaltechTHESIS:04182018-111515439|publisher=California Institute of Technology|date=1982|degree=phd|language=en|first=Barbara Hope|last=Cooper}}</ref>

== Career ==
Cooper stayed at [[California Institute of Technology|Caltech]] until 1983 for a postdoctoral fellowship, then she was hired by Cornell University as an assistant professor.<ref name=":0" /> She was granted full professorship in 1995.<ref name=":3" />

Cooper specialised in charge exchange in low-energy ion-surface scattering. This topic is relevant in fabrication processes based on [[Surface science|surface chemistry]], including plasma etching. She built up her lab from scratch, creating ion-beam systems operating from 10 eV to 1000 eV and other instruments in addition to propelling research into theoretical models.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3" /> She expanded her expertise to include ion erosion and [[X-ray Diffraction|X-ray diffraction]] metal growth.<ref name=":0" /> She was a proponent for multidisciplinary research collaborations at Cornell.<ref name=":2" /> She was a leader in establishing the Cornell Center for Materials Research (CCMR) and the Cornell High-Energy Synchrotron Source (CHESS).<ref name=":0" />

She was interested in science outreach and organised workshops for elementary school students.<ref name=":2" /> She encouraged exploration and the use of interactive examples to teach undergraduate physics. Cooper mentored women in physics and more than half of the graduate students in her research group were women at the time of her death.<ref name=":0" />

== Awards and honours ==

* 1992 [[Maria Goeppert-Mayer Award|Maria Goeppert Mayer Award]] for ''her innovative studies of ion-surface interactions in the hyperthermal energy range. Combining experimental data from a highly versatile ion spectrometer with theoretical modeling, she has developed accurate ion-surface interaction potentials and provided detailed information about energy deposition and scattering mechanisms.''<ref>{{Cite web|title=1992 Maria Goeppert Mayer Award Recipient|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Cooper&first_nm=Barbara&year=1992|url-status=live|access-date=2021-05-06|website=www.aps.org|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110912075926/http://www.aps.org:80/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?first_nm=Barbara&last_nm=Cooper&year=1992 |archive-date=2011-09-12 }}</ref>
* Faculty development awards from [[IBM]] and [[AT&T]].<ref name=":1" />
* 1985 [[National Science Foundation|NSF]] Presidential Young Investigator.<ref name=":1" />
* [[Bell Labs]] Graduate Research Program for Women award.<ref name=":1" />
* Named [[Fellow of the American Physical Society]] in 1995.<ref>{{cite web |title=APS Fellow Archive |url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1995&unit_id=&institution= |website=American Physical Society |at=Filter by Year: 1995 |access-date=8 June 2021}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Cooper was married to physicist Christopher Robert Myers. They had a daughter who was eight at the time of Cooper's death.<ref name=":1" /> Cooper died in 1999 six months after being diagnosed with lung cancer<ref name=":2" /> at [[Cayuga Medical Center]].<ref name=":0" />
